subtype: Approach: assigns jobs by each person's strengths [Thinking]
passage: Sahil, you are captain this year, so hear how Deepak did it at fifteen. Our school was planning Sports Day and I had a list as long as my arm and no idea who should do what. I would have painted the posters myself, badly. Then I thought: who in my class writes like a printed book? Nusrat. And who knows every shopkeeper on the road and could get the permission letters signed at the ward office? Gopal. I did not pick names out of a hat. I went to Nusrat and said, "Your writing is the best in our class, will you do the posters?" Then to Gopal: "You know people, can you get the permissions?" Both said yes at once, because I had named what they were good at. I kept the sports list for myself.

qa.q: Who was asked to do the posters?
qa.a: Nusrat was asked to do the posters.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel at the start, holding a list as long as an arm?
qa.a: Deepak felt overwhelmed and unsure who should do what.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made both classmates say yes, and why?
qa.a: Deepak named what each classmate was good at, so the request felt like a recognition of a real skill.

qa.q: How might Gopal have felt when asked about the permissions?
qa.a: Gopal may have felt pleased and trusted, since the request showed that Deepak had noticed the skill.

grounding: Shows a student captain choosing a poster maker and a permissions person by what each is good at.
